# Your first plot

Time to make a plot. We'll start with an easy question so we can learn the one idea
behind *every* ggplot as we go — the **grammar of graphics**.

> **Question:** what does our experiment look like — how many samples are there in
> each lifestyle?

The plot that answers it is a simple **bar chart**. Building it teaches the grammar we'll
reuse all day.

## Setup {-}

```{r setup02, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)   # here() builds paths from the project root, so they work wherever you run this
meta <- read_tsv(here("project/data", "metadata.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## data → aesthetics → geom {-}

Every ggplot needs three things:

- **data** — the table to plot (`meta`)
- **aesthetics** (`aes`) — which column maps to what (here: `lifestyle` → x-axis)
- **geom** — how to draw it (here: bars)

```{r}
ggplot(meta, aes(x = lifestyle)) +   # data + aesthetic
  geom_bar()                         # geom: one bar per group
```

That's a complete answer: how many samples per lifestyle. 🎉

## Add a layer: another aesthetic {-}

Plots grow by adding more with `+`. Map a **second** variable to the `fill` aesthetic to
also see the timepoints:

```{r}
ggplot(meta, aes(x = lifestyle, fill = timepoint)) +
  geom_bar()
```

## Add labels {-}

`labs()` makes it readable:

```{r}
ggplot(meta, aes(x = lifestyle, fill = timepoint)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Our experiment", x = NULL, y = "Number of samples", fill = "Timepoint")
```

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 The grammar, once and for all:</strong> <code>ggplot(data, aes(...))</code>
  sets the data and the mappings, then you add <code>geom_*()</code> and other layers
  with <code>+</code>. Change the <em>aesthetic</em> or the <em>geom</em> and you change
  the plot — that's all of ggplot.
</div>

<div class="tip">
  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> put an aesthetic like <code>colour</code> or <code>fill</code>
  <em>inside</em> <code>aes()</code> to map it to a column; put it <em>outside</em>
  (e.g. <code>fill = "steelblue"</code>) to set one fixed colour for everything.
</div>

## A different geom: a line {-}

Change the **geom** and you get a different plot from the same grammar. Let's count how
many samples were collected at each timepoint and connect them with a line:

```{r}
meta %>%
  count(timepoint) %>%
  mutate(timepoint = factor(timepoint, levels = c("5h", "10h", "24h"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = timepoint, y = n, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "number of samples")
```

<div class="tip">
  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> timepoints are text, so we make them an ordered
  <code>factor</code> (5 h → 10 h → 24 h); <code>group = 1</code> tells ggplot to connect
  the points into one line. (You'll draw a line <em>per group</em> later, when you track a
  gene across conditions — there the lines really differ.)
</div>

## Change the whole look: themes {-}

Every plot has a **theme** — the styling of everything that isn't the data (background,
grid lines, fonts). Swap the theme to restyle the whole plot in one line. Save the plot to
an object first, then try a few:

```{r}
p <- ggplot(meta, aes(x = lifestyle, fill = timepoint)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Our experiment", x = NULL, y = "Number of samples")

p + theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
p + theme_classic()
```

```{r}
p + theme_bw()
```

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Principle:</strong> a <code>theme_*()</code> restyles the non-data parts of a
  plot in one line. Pick one you like (<code>theme_minimal()</code>,
  <code>theme_classic()</code>, <code>theme_bw()</code>, <code>theme_void()</code>…), or set
  it for the whole session with <code>theme_set(theme_minimal())</code>.
</div>

### 👉 Your turn {-}

Make a bar chart with **`timepoint`** on the x-axis, filled by **`lifestyle`**, with nice
labels — then **apply a theme** you like.

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(meta, aes(x = timepoint, fill = lifestyle)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Timepoint", y = "Number of samples", fill = "Lifestyle") +
  theme_minimal()
```
</details>

> 🤖 **Ask your AI:** *"How do I turn this ggplot bar chart into a horizontal one, and
> change the bars to a custom colour palette?"*
